extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate calculus instructors, mathematics-education researchers, and curriculum designers (including client-discipline faculty who use calculus)
extracted.subtask_short: designing tasks to elicit calculus understanding
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and evaluating prototype tasks and descriptions that elicit, document, and measure undergraduate students' understanding of fundamental calculus concepts (as viewed by calculus teachers and by client-discipline users).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of fundamental calculus concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the small set of calculus concepts faculty agree are essential (e.g., function, limit, derivative, integral; also infinitesimals, infinity, sequences/series, Riemann sums, differential equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study seeks a concise list (products: 1) a determination of the fundamental calculus concepts). Note discipline differences: client disciplines commonly emphasize function, derivative, and integral; some client instructors de-emphasize 'limit' unless needed for derivative definition. Use faculty input from both mathematics and client disciplines to refine the core set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding calculus beyond computations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Understanding calculus beyond computations" is defined as an intertwining of computational skill and conceptual understanding — the relationship between skill and understanding that gives power of application in varied settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks and assessments should not only check procedural computation but probe whether students can apply, adjust, and remember skills in novel contexts. Quote from paper: 'In order to learn skills... they must be learned with understanding' (Hiebert et al., 1997). Design tasks that require both skill and conceptual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers' view of understanding — 'HOW and WHY'
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers of calculus characterize understanding as knowing how to carry out procedures (procedural fluency) and why procedures work (procedural application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess via written tasks or oral questions that walk students through procedures (example Figure 1: derivative→extrema→second derivative→inflection→graph without technology). Tasks are often theoretical/abstract and contrived to access specific procedures. Scoring should value flexible, accurate, efficient execution and the ability to discuss when/why a procedure applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Users' view of understanding — 'WHICH and WHY'
rubrics_metrics.description: Client-discipline users view understanding as recognizing which calculus concept/tool applies (relational understanding) and why it applies, including predictive power about real-world behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit with written, discipline-situated tasks (example Figure 2: electric field accumulation requiring an integral) that require mapping physical meaning to mathematical objects, selecting appropriate tools, and making sensible predictions. Scoring should prioritize correct model selection, interpretation of variables, and ability to judge plausibility of results in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4-part framework for eliciting and evaluating understanding (situation, library, procedures, predictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding is modeled as a process with four components: Situation (recognize the expected concept), Library (select appropriate description/model), Procedures and Methods (execute linked procedures accurately), Predictions (make sensible predictions and sanity checks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four corners as assessment dimensions: whether students identify the situation type, choose an appropriate model from their 'library', carry out the method correctly, and interpret/check the prediction (units, reasonableness). Both teachers' and users' views can be expressed within this framework; tasks should allow scoring across these dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized deeper-understanding framework (realistic situations & construction of description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher-level understanding involves: giving realistic situations that don't neatly fit existing descriptions; students composing their own description/model; linking concepts to procedures; making sensible predictions and relating results back to assumptions and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that resist pattern-matching and require students to construct descriptions (not just choose from a library). Scoring should reward articulation of modeling assumptions, consideration of margins of error, and sensitivity to changing assumptions — indicators of transfer and deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task context: contrived vs realistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks may be contrived (theoretical/abstract, formatted to fit existing descriptions) or realistic (raw situations that may not fit library descriptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrived tasks (used often by teachers) are useful to teach and assess procedural fluency but risk promoting pattern-matching without transfer. Realistic tasks (favored in the hypothesized view) are better for assessing ability to model novel situations and to transfer calculus to client-discipline problems. Balance both types depending on the targeted dimension of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicitation methods: written tasks and oral questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers primarily use written tasks (and oral questions) that guide students through steps; users use written, discipline-specific tasks that embed necessary domain information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select elicitation method to match the targeted understanding: oral/written stepwise tasks to probe procedural fluency and reasoning steps; written, context-rich tasks to probe model selection and interpretation. Include domain scaffolding when students lack prior discipline knowledge (as in Figure 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and notation choices to reinforce meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of verbiage and notation affects student understanding: client instructors often use 'rate of change,' 'summation,' 'accumulation' rather than 'derivative'/'integral' to emphasize physical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching novices, choose language and notation that connects to physical interpretation; in assessment tasks, consider the audience and whether to require formal terminology or accept discipline-reinforcing vocabulary. In industry contexts, formal terms may be appropriate once peers share understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment validity for real-world application (transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A in calculus (procedural proficiency) does not necessarily indicate ability to apply calculus sensibly in client-discipline contexts; assessments must measure transfer and predictive interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks that require stepping out of pure mathematics to evaluate real-world plausibility, check units, and reflect on assumptions. Scoring should separate procedural correctness from the ability to interpret and justify results in application contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-research process for task development
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an iterative, multi-tier design research approach: work with presumed experts to generate prototype tasks, run cycles that include diversity, selection, and accumulation, and refine tasks through faculty and student interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit faculty (math and client disciplines) as presumed experts, run intradisciplinary then interdisciplinary cycles, collect student work to test tasks, and refine tasks across cycles. Evaluate tasks for their ability to elicit the targeted dimensions of understanding rather than for generalizable student population claims in early cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disciplinary differences in emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Different client disciplines prioritize different calculus concepts and framings (e.g., physics/operations research may 'wash out' limit; engineering and math highlight limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing tasks for cross-disciplinary curricula, be explicit about which conceptual emphases are required by the target discipline and tailor tasks/language accordingly. Use faculty input from the target client discipline to ensure relevance and appropriate framing.
